extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the validity and epistemic weight of deductive inferences, the status of axioms and assumptions, and the limits of tests like 'inconceivability' when used to establish truth. Focuses on how to assess premises, the role of experience, and common confusions (conception vs belief).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty limited to pure number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) applies only to propositions about pure Number, and only so long as numbers are not taken as precise indices of actual quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arithmetic conclusions are used to infer equality or inequality in other respects, one must assume all units are equal in that respect (e.g., two pounds being equal assumes identical pound-standards). In cases involving measurement or physical quantities, treat arithmetic-derived conclusions as hypothetical: check the hidden assumption that units are equivalent, and expect observational testing and approximation rather than categorical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive (demonstrative) sciences proceed by tracing consequences of certain assumptions and are therefore hypothetical: they separate deriving inferences from judging the truth of the assumptions themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should split into two tasks: (1) ascertain how nearly the assumptions are true for the case at hand (typically by observation or case-specific argument), and (2) determine once-for-all what follows from those assumptions. Prepare deductive results for reuse but always verify the applicability of premises empirically when moving to particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid deduction does not ensure factual truth of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of propositions may be perfectly deduced from false assumptions; deduction secures validity of inference, not truth of premises or real-world applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect premises independently. Historical examples (e.g., Ptolemaic or Cartesian synthetic systems) show elaborate consistent deductions can arise from false starting assumptions. Use reductio ad absurdum to expose false premises by deriving contradictions with known facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept inconceivability of negation as a sufficient test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconceivableness of the negation of a proposition is not by itself a reliable proof of its truth, because inconceivableness can arise from causes other than uniform experience (tradition, strong association, limited imagination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to ground assurance in the actual uniformity of past experience (when appropriate) rather than inferring such uniformity from psychological inability to conceive the contrary. Examine whether alleged inconceivableness truly reflects comprehensive experience or only habit, association, or historical limitation (examples: antipodes, motion of the earth vs sun). Recognize occasional failures of inconceivability do not uniquely discredit other tests; instead evaluate the source and weight of the alleged inconceivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'inconceivable' as inability to form an idea vs inability to believe
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'inconceivable' can mean either inability to form a conception (idea) or inability to hold a belief; conflating these senses corrupts arguments that rely on inconceivability as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using inconceivability as a test, specify which sense is intended. Examples: antipodes were imaginable (idea possible) but unbelievable; the 'end of extension' is unimaginable (idea fails). Arguments must not slide between 'cannot imagine' and 'cannot believe' without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: When assessing multi-step arguments, check for new uncertain premises rather than penalizing length alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the same axiom or postulate across many inferential steps does not multiply chances of error if no new premises are introduced; an argument's length alone does not necessarily reduce reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether intermediate steps introduce distinct, independent assumptions of uncertain truth. If they do, each adds a potential source of error; if they merely reuse the same justified axiom, the number of steps does not proportionally increase risk. Thus focus on the character and independence of premises taken on at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct evidence of uniformity of experience to second-hand psychological tests
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposition is said to be justified because its negation is inconceivable, the real justificatory ground should be the underlying uniformity of experience; rely on that where accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the uniformity explicit and evaluate its strength (strong, weak, negligible). Examples show uniform experience can be either decisive (e.g., 'two straight lines cannot inclose a space' as tied to pervasive experience) or misleading (e.g., 'all swans are white' overturned by new facts). Do not substitute a psychological test for the substantive empirical record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between self-evident subjective facts and claims about external reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate sensations and states of consciousness (I feel cold) have a stronger claim to being incorrigible than beliefs about external objects; the inconceivableness test is more defensible for self-perception than for noumenal claims about external reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, treat subjective present sensations as 'known per se' and not in need of the same external evidential support. Conversely, beliefs about matter, space, time as objective realities require argument and cannot be settled solely by alleged inconceivableness, because reasonable dissenters may hold the negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically test how far assumptions fail in each particular case
rubrics_metrics.description: In non-numerical deductive applications, determining the extent to which assumptions are not exactly true is typically an empirical question that must be re-examined for each new case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a one-size-fits-all tolerable approximation: repeated observation or case-specific argument may be required, and different instances may present varying degrees of difficulty. Record and report the degree of approximation and how it impacts the validity of conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify conceptual usage before using it in epistemic arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that rely on concepts (e.g., 'inconceivability', 'belief', 'conception') must define and use them consistently; equivocation undermines the argumentative force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating philosophical or methodological claims, revise language to preserve distinctions (e.g., 'I can conceive X' vs 'I can believe X'). Explicitly state whether tests aim at forming ideas, eliciting belief, or detecting psychological inevitability, and show how that target bears on objective truth.
